item.title: CVSS 3.1 calculator
item.description:
What the score means#

CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) measures the technical severity of a vulnerability, not the risk it poses to you. A 9.8 in a library you never load is less urgent than a 6.5 on your internet-facing login page. Use the base score to describe the vulnerability itself, and the environmental metrics to say what it means for a specific system.

The three metric groups#

  • Base metrics describe the vulnerability itself: how it is reached, what the attacker needs, and what it breaks. They don’t change over time or between environments, and they are what belongs in an advisory or a pentest finding.
  • Temporal metrics describe how the picture changes over time: whether working exploit code exists, whether a fix is available, and how well confirmed the report is. They can only lower the score.
  • Environmental metrics adapt the score to one environment. The requirements say how much confidentiality, integrity and availability matter for the affected asset; the modified metrics account for controls you already have. A service that is only reachable from the same network segment, for example, can set Modified Attack Vector to Adjacent. These can raise or lower the score.

Where scores usually go wrong#

  • Scope is Changed only when the vulnerable component and the impacted component sit under different security authorities: stored XSS (the web application is vulnerable, the victim’s browser is impacted) or a virtual machine escape. It is not a way of saying “this one is serious”.
  • Privileges Required is what the attacker needs before the attack, not what they gain from it.
  • Attack Complexity is about conditions outside the attacker’s control, such as winning a race or needing a man-in-the-middle position. It is not about how hard the exploit was to write.
  • User Interaction is Required when someone other than the attacker has to do something, for example click a link or open a file.
  • One vulnerability, one score. Score the flaw you found, not the whole attack chain an attacker could build from it.

Why 3.1 first#

CVSS 4.0 fixes several of the weaknesses above, but a large share of scanner output, existing advisories and report templates still use 3.1. A 4.0 calculator will follow.

item.title: JWT inspector
item.description:
A token is a credential#

A JSON Web Token (JWT) in an Authorization header is as good as a password for as long as it is valid. Pasting it into an online decoder hands that credential to a third party, and to everything in between: the site’s logs, its analytics, the browser extensions on the page.

This inspector runs entirely in your browser. It makes no network requests, and it keeps the token out of the URL, the browser history and local storage. Spellchecking is switched off in the input fields, because some browsers send the text of spellchecked fields to a cloud service.

item.title: Before your interview: what happens when you type a URL, security edition
item.description:
“What happens when you type a URL into the browser and press Enter?” is the most common open question in web security interviews, for pentester, AppSec and security engineer roles alike. It sounds like a networking quiz. It isn’t one.

The interviewer wants to see two things. First, whether you can hold a whole system in your head, from a keystroke to pixels. Second, and this is what separates a security answer from a networking answer, whether you notice that every hop is a trust decision: something tells the browser where to go, something proves who is on the other end, and something decides what the page is allowed to do. Each of those can lie, and each has a control with a known limit.

item.title: Pentmax devlog #0: planning before the first line of code
item.description: Pentmax is my first open source project: a self-hosted platform that follows a penetration test from scope to sign-off. This first devlog entry contains no code, and that is deliberate. Phase 0 produced a planning document, a roadmap and twelve Architecture Decision Records (ADRs: short documents that record one decision, its context and its consequences). The most valuable outcome was not a decision I made but one I reversed: the first design was built for the wrong user.

item.title: Pentmax
item.description:
Pentmax is a self-hosted web application that carries a penetration test from scope to sign-off: scoping, authorization, testing, findings, reporting, delivery, remediation and retest. It is built for solo testers and small teams of one to ten people.

The problem#

A pentest platform holds the most sensitive data a client will ever hand over: confirmed vulnerabilities, working exploit paths, test credentials, screenshots of internal systems. In a small team that data is rarely in one place. Findings sit in a reporting tool, the scope in a spreadsheet, the authorization in an email or in someone’s memory of a phone call, and the client’s credentials in a messenger.

item.title: Colophon
item.description:
This site practices what it preaches.

Built with#

  • Hugo, a static site generator. There is no server-side code, no database and no admin panel to attack.
  • A hand-written theme called Redacted. Type is set in Source Serif 4 and JetBrains Mono, both under the SIL Open Font License.
  • Deployed with GitHub Actions to GitHub Pages.

What it does not do#

  • No trackers, no analytics, no cookies.
  • No third-party requests. Fonts, styles and scripts are served from this origin.
  • No inline scripts or styles. Every script is a separate file from this origin, and each has one job:
    • a small theme toggle;
    • search, built on Pagefind. The index is generated at build time and searched in your browser, so your queries never leave it;
    • one script per tool. The tools run entirely in your browser and make no network requests: a token or vector you paste in stays on your machine.

Hardening#

  • A strict Content Security Policy: default-src 'none', with script-src, style-src and font-src limited to 'self'. The one addition is 'wasm-unsafe-eval', which search needs to compile its WebAssembly module. It does not allow JavaScript eval.
  • The stylesheet and every script are fingerprinted and loaded with Subresource Integrity (sha384).
  • A security.txt (RFC 9116) for reporting vulnerabilities.

Labels you’ll see#

Posts carry a TLP label (Traffic Light Protocol 2.0). Everything published here is TLP:CLEAR or TLP:GREEN by nature, but the label tells you how the source material was originally shared. Advisories also show a severity and, where available, a CVSS score.

item.title: whoami
item.description:
I’m synt0x, a security engineer who spent the first part of my career as a software developer.

For years I built software: I designed it, wrote it, shipped it under deadlines and kept it running in production. Now I break it and help fix it. Knowing how software is actually built helps on both sides of that work: I know where to look for the weak spots, and I know what a fix has to look like for a development team to adopt it. I aim for findings that lead to real fixes, not findings that only look good in a report.
